newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya shilling falls further, stays under pressure.
newsitem.headline: Kenya shilling falls further, stays under pressure.

text.p: The Kenyan shilling suffered further losses versus the dollar on Monday and remained under pressure on heavy demand for dollars by nervous investors after the IMF cancelled a key aid package.

Commercial bank dealers said despite slow trading on Monday, the shilling looked weak in the near term. They said it was trading at 62.50/63.50 against an opening rate of 61.50/63.50, a decline of around 3.25 percent.
"The market's still very nervous, we're receiving a lot of inquiries," said a senior dealer.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) decision to suspend a $205 million three-year loan under its Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF) in a row over corruption severely shook Kenya's foreign exchange and equity markets on Friday.
The shilling fell to as low as 64.50 on Friday after opening at 59.50 but rebounded to close at about 61.50 on the dollar.
Dealers said the shilling's future was bleak and they were keeping wide spreads because the market was so nervous. They said that it was unusually difficult to forecast trade volumes.
"Pressure is there. Orders are large," one commercial dealer said, adding that orders were around $10-$20 million and were from both offshore investors and commercial companies.
But some market analysts said the shilling's misfortune -- a drop to levels above 60 was a blessing in disguise.
"The shilling is now at a level that exporters can live with," said an investment analyst from Loita Asset Management.
"At this level it will be of immense use to our own people," added the investment analyst, who declined to be named.
An official from the Coffee Board of Kenya told Reuters that farmers would benefit from the fall in the shilling as auction prices were denominated in dollars.

"Because we are selling the coffee at the auctions in dollars, it could be leading to a boom for the farmer, at least for those who are selling their coffee this week and the next few weeks the shilling rate should be quite good," he said.
For a long time exporters have complained that the shilling was far too strong, saying the 53-55 band where it had held for a long time, was not competitive enough.
For many, such as the Eastern Africa Association that groups British companies, a rate in the range of 65 was preferable.
"The big question is how it has gotten here. The problem is it might not be stable because of the volatility in the market which is not good for any business planning," one analyst said.
On Friday, Kenyan Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi said that the government would let market forces determine shilling direction but it still hoped to maintain price stability.

Speaking also on Friday, Central Bank of Kenya Governor Micah Cheserem said it was not prudent for the central bank to intervene to stem the shilling slide. He said joining a stampede was likely to only further fuel shilling losses.
In his first comment on the IMF ruling, President Daniel arap Moi said on Sunday that "the stoppage of financial aid to Kenya by the IMF was purely political and has no economic rationality."
